question: Why are you exploring new opportunities?
answer: I left KKday in August 2026. The Shanghai office cut many jobs, and I was one of them. So I'm using this time to choose carefully. I'm looking for three things. First, AI on mobile is the core product, not a side feature. Second, I own the Android experience from start to finish. Third, a small team where I work closely with backend and AI engineers. At KKday, I worked on both sides of an AI feature. How the planner built an answer, and how a traveler actually used it. I want more of that, on Android. ActAI fits all three.

question: Why do you want to join ActAI specifically?
answer: There are three reasons. First, ActAI's product and my own product share a similar direction. In May, I started designing an AI agent in my spare time. It's called Cabinet. For example, I plan a three-day trip. I need to check my calendar, the weather, and my budget. Checking them one by one is slow. And I can easily miss something. Cabinet thinks of all this for me. Then it gives me a good plan. ActAI builds proactive AI products for everyone. People don't need to write complex prompts. The first product starts with communication. It puts an agent at the center. The goal is to make coordination between people easier. Here is my understanding. Friends agree on a Friday meeting in a chat. Then the agent sets it up for them. So I have real interest in this direction. I also have real experience. Second, ActAI needs someone to make AI fast and stable on Android. That's my strength. I have ten years of experience, mostly on Android. At KKday, I cut the first-screen loading time on Android. It went from three seconds to under one second. I also showed AI results step by step. Users didn't have to wait. At Ping An Haoxue, I improved a classroom app on cheap Android tablets. It ran smoothly, even on low-end devices. Third, I want to join a startup like ActAI. In a startup, nobody writes every detail for you. You need to bring structure, make decisions, and move fast. I like this way of working. I can help shape the product. And I own the results. I've done this before. At Kezhi, the product was brand new. I reported to the CTO. I was the only Android engineer. I built the whole Android app myself, from zero to launch, in four weeks. So I want to build a great product with ActAI. I want people to trust it and use it every day.

question: Why did you leave your last three companies?
answer: Just to be precise, two of them were layoffs, and one was my own decision. At KKday, the business line was shrinking. Most of the people they kept had been there longer than me. I'd joined about a year and a half earlier. My performance was in the top 30% of the Tour team, so I don't think it was about my work. Debon was similar. The business had struggled for two years, and our Android team went from three people to one. They kept the longest-serving engineer. Before I left, my work had shipped and I handed everything over cleanly. Kezhi was different. After the team was disbanded, there was no real product work left, and the company's future was unclear. Many people left, and I decided to leave too.

question: What people or working styles do you dislike working with, especially in your most recent role?
answer: I don't like it when people change something others depend on, and don't tell them. Once, we were building a booking page. The backend changed how stock status was returned, but didn't tell the Android side. So some packages that were in stock couldn't be selected. I compared the real response with what we had agreed, and found the change. Then I worked with the backend engineer on the fix. We retested every package that was affected. After that, we agreed on one rule. For any shared API change, explain what changed first, and send sample data. That way, the app side can check the impact. Later, when they changed these APIs, they sent sample data first. So we found what both sides needed to change before testing together. I understand things get missed under deadlines. When I do backend work, I remind myself of this too. When your change affects others, telling them early is a habit I value.

question: What kind of manager do you work best with?
answer: I value open, direct communication, and I can adapt to different management styles. Some managers give detailed tasks, while others start with a broad direction. I don't wait for every detail to be defined. I try to understand what they want to achieve and why, then think about the user's needs and the technical options. I bring my understanding, a proposed approach and a next step to discuss and confirm. As the work moves forward, I share progress, raise risks early, and adjust based on feedback. I see helping turn a broad direction into a practical result as part of my responsibility.

question: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
answer: I'm good at following a problem across the app and the backend. At KKday, sometimes the AI reply didn't fit what the app could show. I could fix both the reply format and the fallback. My weak spot is model training. I'm better at putting AI into products. I can own the app side and the test cases. For model quality, I'd work with the ML engineer.

question: What do you understand about the product we're building, and what would you still need to learn?
answer: Based on your introduction, ActAI brings AI into everyday voice and text communication. It aims to understand what people need and help them take the next steps. I believe in this direction. People chat every day, and many tasks start in a chat. For example, friends agree to meet on Friday. Then someone still has to confirm the time and add it to a calendar. I see a real chance for AI to help with those steps. I worked on AI trip planning at KKday, and I'm building Cabinet, my own assistant app. So I understand the product side. What I'd still need to learn is your users and your first use case. Which task matters most right now, and how do you decide when the assistant should act and when it should ask? I'd also want to learn your AI stack and how the Android app talks to it. On the technical side, I have little hands-on experience with on-device ML, like TensorFlow Lite or ML Kit. I'd build a small working example with your models in my first month and pair with the ML engineer.

question: How do you feel about work-life balance? What if priorities change halfway through a sprint?
answer: I'm comfortable with a fast pace and intense sprints. I understand that in a startup, priorities can change as we learn more about users. If priorities change halfway through a sprint, I'd first understand the new goal and agree with the team on what comes first. Then I'd check what work we can reuse, what needs to change, and what can wait. I'd update the people affected so everyone knows the new plan. I also look for risks and blockers early, especially where my work depends on other people or systems. If I spot a problem, I won't leave it until the deadline. I'll investigate early, tell the people involved, and work with them to solve it quickly. If we need help or a decision, I'll ask early so the work can keep moving. For an important launch, I'm willing to put in extra time. I'd focus on getting the essential user flow working and tested, and follow through until the issues are resolved.

question: We look for 7H: head, hands, hustle, humility, heart, hunger and habits. Which one describes you best? Give an example.
answer: I'd choose Hands, because I enjoy turning ideas into working products. At Kezhi, we had four weeks to launch the first version of an education app. I was the only Android engineer, responsible for architecture, development, testing and release. Some features already existed as web pages. Instead of rebuilding everything in native Android, I integrated those pages into the app. That helped us focus our time on the essential work and launch within four weeks. That experience reflects how I work: understand the goal, make practical trade-offs, and take responsibility through delivery. I'd love to bring that approach to ActAI.

question: If you work remotely, how do you keep yourself accountable daily and weekly? What is on your personal scoreboard?
answer: At KKday, I worked remotely some of the time. I plan each week around handoff points. For a booking page, I first agree when we test with the backend, and when QA gets it. Then I plan my own coding time around that. Each day follows those points. If we test with the backend in the afternoon, I get the flow working in the morning and list the API issues. So we can fix them together right away. My updates are specific. For example: "The page is done. The main flow works. Empty stock is left. I'll check it with the backend tomorrow." That way, QA knows what they can test first. Across time zones, I'd write the questions, sample data, and what needs confirming clearly in advance. Then we'd use the overlap hours to discuss them together. When something urgent comes in, I explain the trade-off. For example: "Today I'll fix the checkout bug. The page redesign moves one day. I'll send the new QA date." Then I confirm it with my lead. Each week, I check three things. Did I deliver what I promised? How much was missed or redone? Did anyone wait on me?

question: Would you deliver bad news to your team early or later?
answer: Early. The sooner the team knows, the more time they have to adjust. But I bring the problem and a suggestion together. At Debon Securities, I was rebuilding part of our trading app. It was planned to ship with that week's release. During testing, I found some old pages had a broken back button with the new navigation. I hadn't checked every page yet. But it could already affect the release. So I told the project manager that same day. I said: "Some pages are confirmed broken. I'm still checking the rest. If this ships this week, we may not have time to test it fully. I suggest we keep the old pages, and move this change to the next release. Everything else can ship as planned. I'll update you tomorrow afternoon on the impact and the fix." We changed the release scope. Everything else shipped on time. My change shipped later, after it was fixed and tested. To me, telling early gives the team time to choose. And I don't just report the problem. I keep pushing the fix, and keep everyone updated.

So I care a lot about waiting time in AI apps too. This role is about lower latency and a better real experience on Android. That's exactly the kind of work that drives me.

question: Who do you think would use this product, and what problem would it solve for them?
answer: Based on your introduction, I think ActAI is for anyone who coordinates with other people every day: friends, families and small teams. Take a meeting across time zones. Today someone has to work out the time, create the event, send the invite and check everyone got it. ActAI could draft the invite, ask one short question if the time zone is unclear, and send it after the user confirms. If the connection drops, it should show clearly whether the invite went out. People would use it because it saves those follow-up steps every day, not because it has more AI features.

question: How would you explain the idea of 'Cursor for everyone' in practical user terms?
answer: I understand "Cursor for everyone" as giving ordinary people the kind of help Cursor gives programmers. Cursor helps a developer turn an idea into working software with AI. For everyone else, the same idea means you say what you want in everyday language, and the AI helps you get it done. Starting with communication makes sense to me. Friends agree to meet on Friday in a chat. After that, someone still has to confirm the time, add it to a calendar and set a reminder. ActAI could handle those steps for them. People wouldn't need to learn complex prompts. They'd just speak naturally. The assistant would use the context, do the task, and ask when a decision needs the user. That's why I'm excited about this direction.

question: How has your agent or RAG work changed the way you build mobile experiences?

So on Android, I now plan for slow answers, wrong answers and unclear states from the start.

question: Tell me about a project you owned from an unclear problem through delivery.
answer: The clearest one is the AI trip planner at KKday. The goal was simple to say but unclear to build: help travelers plan a trip they can actually book. Planning by hand was slow, so I designed how the agent works, connected it to our real product and order data, and built the core backend. I also agreed with the app team how a day card and a map point should look, so the app could show day one first. When a plan failed our checks, it retried, then fell back to a safe default. In the end it handled about 300,000 trip plans a day.

question: Which achievement are you most proud of, and how did you measure its impact?
answer: The product page at KKday. When a traveller tapped a tour, it took about a second before the options and prices appeared. I found the app was reading the same data again and again and doing heavy work when the page opened. So I prepared the price and stock lookups in advance, moved the heavy work to the background, and cached the results. It went from about one second to about 300 milliseconds. I measured it by timing the tap to the finished screen, and I went through the booking flow myself afterwards to feel the difference.

question: Tell me about a time you solved a problem outside your formal responsibilities.
answer: At KKday, I noticed that project information was spread across different places. Requirements, designs and API details were hard to find, and people had to ask around. Some gaps only showed up during integration or testing. So I proposed one Slack channel for each project, with the owners from product, design, Android, iOS and backend. We also used one Confluence page for requirements, designs, development plans and test cases. When something changed, we updated the page first, then told the owners. This made information easier to find and helped us spot differences in understanding earlier. I later shared the approach at the monthly tech sharing session I organized, and other teams started using it too. My role was Android development, but I wanted to help with a problem that affected the whole team's delivery.

question: Tell me about a project that did not achieve the result you expected.
answer: I'd talk about the AI homework-grading product at Kezhi. I was responsible for Android and the multi-subject RAG work. The first version was live. It could grade an assignment in a few seconds. But it didn't yet give teachers enough help with targeted teaching. It handled one assignment at a time. It didn't group and study each student's past mistakes. Teachers could see today's wrong answers. But they couldn't easily see repeated mistakes or decide what to teach next. I hadn't thought enough about how teachers would use the results after grading. Fast grading was useful. But teachers also needed a clear picture across several assignments. If I planned it again, I'd include past mistakes and group them by knowledge point from the start. Then I'd add summaries of weak areas. I'd check the quality of the analysis, whether teachers used it, and whether students made fewer similar mistakes. The lesson was to think through the full workflow. After AI gives a result, how does it help the user take the next step?

question: Tell me about a time you had to move fast.
answer: At Kezhi, I was the only Android engineer, and I built the whole Android app for an exam-prep product from zero to launch in four weeks. Back then, AI coding tools weren't good enough, so I wrote and worked out almost all of it myself. Some screens were in the app, and some were web pages. So I set up routing between modules. I also made a way to show web pages inside the app. That way, both kinds of features made the first version.

question: What would you do if you couldn't stop feature work to fix reliability?
answer: I faced that at Debon. The trading app still needed new features while we improved its architecture and fixed crashes. So I did both: I built the watchlist, moved shared network code into one place, and fixed crashes group by group, the most common first. Over time, the team cut the crash rate to about one tenth. Here, if users were losing messages, I'd fix that path first and keep other work moving.

question: How do you handle a short period of intense work before a critical launch?
answer: I'm comfortable with a short period of intense work before an important launch. I'd confirm what must be ready, focus on the core user flow, and agree with the team on what can wait. I'd check risky parts and dependencies early, so problems don't pile up at the end. If something goes wrong, I'd investigate right away, involve the right people, and work through it quickly. I'd keep the team updated and ask for help early if needed. I'm willing to put in extra time to help us deliver. I'd still test the core flow and verify the fixes, so we can move fast and release something users can rely on.

question: How would you respond if a founder changed direction after two weeks of your work?
answer: First, I'd understand why the direction changed and what we're trying to achieve now. In a startup, new information can change the plan, and that's normal. Then I'd review the work already done: what we can reuse, what needs to change, and what we should stop. I'd share the impact on timing and any big risks early, and agree with the founder on the next priority. Once we're aligned, I'd adjust quickly and start moving. I wouldn't keep building the old plan just because I'd spent two weeks on it. I'd check the biggest unknowns early and share progress, so we can find problems and solve them fast.

question: What's the biggest risk you see in joining us?
expected: 坦诚提到早期产品可能转向；看核心团队是否还在
answer: The biggest risk is that I can't see the product yet, so I might build the wrong thing first. I'd reduce that risk by using the app myself, asking which user task matters most, and shipping a small version early to learn from real use.

question: How do you handle stress and pressure?
expected: 拆分优先级、沟通风险；可带上线前冲刺
answer: I handle stress by making a plan and focusing on the next step. At KKday, when a launch was tight, I split the work into small parts and checked the risky ones first. I also told the team early when something might slip. That way, pressure didn't turn into surprises.

question: How do you keep up with changes in Android and AI?
expected: 实际使用 Codex/Claude 等，CabinetAI 业余验证新技术
answer: Mostly by building. I use AI coding tools every day, and I read the official Android and model docs when something changes. I also try new things in CabinetAI first, so I know what's worth using at work.

question: Tell me about a time you had to say no to a product manager.
expected: 先确认核心体验与本版必须项，给出选项而非直接拒绝
answer: At KKday, a product colleague wanted to ship a booking page on the planned date, but I found a data problem with out-of-stock items. I said no to the full release. I explained the risk and suggested we ship the main flow and move that part to the next release. We agreed, and QA got a clear date.

question: If you joined us, what would you do in your first 30 days?
expected: 了解产品与用户、熟悉代码与发布流程、尽快交付一个小改动
answer: In my first 30 days, I'd focus on learning the product and shipping something small. First, I'd use the app myself every day, on a normal phone and a weak network. I'd note where I wait, where I'm not sure what happened, and where I had to fix something by hand. Then I'd ask the team which user task matters most right now. Second, I'd get the Android build running and go through the full flow: voice input, streaming answers, and actions the user confirms. I'd check the basics early, like what happens when the network drops or the app is killed in the background. Third, I'd pick one small, real improvement and ship it. For example, making the first answer appear faster, or showing clearly whether an action worked. I'd want real feedback from use, not just my own opinion. By day 30, I'd like to say: I understand the core flow, I've shipped one useful change, and I know which problem to own next.

question: How do you prioritize when everything seems urgent?
expected: 按用户影响与可逆性排序，和 PM/负责人对齐
answer: I start with what's most urgent for users, not what's loudest. I ask what breaks if this waits a day, and what breaks if it ships wrong. Then I sort the work into three groups: things that block other people, things that affect users right now, and things that can wait. I tell the people affected what moves and when, so nobody is guessing. At KKday, when a checkout issue landed in the middle of a page redesign, I fixed checkout first and told my lead and QA the new date for the redesign.

question: How would you feel about being the only Android engineer on the team?
expected: 可之时就是唯一 Android 工程师，四周上线，也负责测试与发布
answer: I'd be comfortable with it, because I've done it before. At Kezhi, I was the only Android engineer, and I built the whole Android app from zero to launch in four weeks. I handled the architecture, the coding, testing and the release myself. There are two things I'd do to make it work well. First, I'd keep the Android side easy for others to pick up. I'd write clear notes on the build, the release steps and the main flows, so the team isn't blocked when I'm away. Second, I'd stay close to the backend and AI engineers. When the app and the AI disagree about a reply, I'd rather fix it with them early than find it at release. I also like this setup. You see the whole product, and you can move fast. So I'd be happy to own the Android side here.

question: What would you do if you disagreed with the CTO's technical decision?
expected: 私下带数据/取舍沟通，决定后全力执行
answer: I'd share my concern early and privately, with facts. I'd say what I'm worried about, what it means for users or the date, and one other option. Then I'd listen, because the CTO sees things I don't. Once we decide, I'd support it fully and own my part.

question: How would you give feedback to a teammate whose code quality is poor?
expected: 私下、具体、对事不对人，结合 review
answer: I'd start privately and with a question, not a judgment. I'd ask what they were trying to do in that code, and point to one concrete example. For instance: "This function does three things at once. Could we split it, so it's easier to test?" I'd offer to pair on it, because showing is better than telling. I'd focus on the code, not the person, and I'd keep it between us first. If the same problem kept coming back, I'd agree on a simple standard with the team, like a review checklist.

question: Tell me about a time you led a change without formal authority.
expected: KKday 一个 Slack 频道 + 一份 Confluence 文档，分享会推广
answer: At Debon Securities, I led the move to a cleaner Android architecture without being anyone's manager. I didn't ask for a big rewrite. I moved one module to MVVM first, while we kept shipping features. Then I showed the team it was easier to change and test. After that, I ran training sessions, and the team moved more modules step by step.

question: What does ownership mean to you?
expected: 从问题到上线后结果都负责；可之独立交付
answer: Ownership means I own the result, not just my code. If something I built breaks for users, I fix it and tell the team early. At Kezhi, I was the only Android engineer, so I owned the app from the first design to launch and testing. I also keep improving it after launch, not just when the ticket closes.

question: Some meetings might be late in the evening because of time zones. Is that OK for you?

answer: Yes, that's fine. I'd plan those calls in advance and keep the rest of my work in writing, so late meetings don't slow the team down.

question: If we made you an offer today, would you accept it?

answer: Yes, I would. I want to join ActAI, and this role is exactly the mix of Android and AI work I'm looking for. I'd just like to see the full offer in writing first, including the guaranteed months and any bonus, so I can give you a clear answer within a few days.

question: Your last role was about a year and a half. Why should we believe you'll stay longer?

answer: I spent almost six years at Ping An, from 2015 to 2021, so I do stay when the work and the team are right. My last two short roles ended in layoffs, not by my choice. I'm looking for a place where I can own the Android side for years, and ActAI is that place for me.

question: What's the last thing you built just for fun or to learn?

I used AI coding tools for the simpler screens, which saved a lot of time. It isn't on Google Play yet, because I'm still finishing the integration testing. The iOS build just reached testing first.

question: Our first version gets bad reviews on Google Play. What do you do?
expected: 分类评论、看数据、修最痛的问题、回复用户
answer: I'd take the bad reviews seriously and look at them the same day. First, I'd read the reviews and group them: crashes, slow answers, unclear results, or missing features. Then I'd check the crash reports and the worst cases myself, on a normal phone and a weak network. I'd fix the most common problem first and ship a small update fast. I'd also reply to reviewers honestly and tell them what we fixed. Bad reviews are useful feedback, so I'd keep watching them every week.

question: How do you feel about a paid trial project before an offer?
expected: 愿意，确认范围与时长
answer: Yes, I'm happy to do a paid trial project. It's a fair way for both of us to see how I work before we commit. I'd want a clear, small task with a real goal and a time limit, and I'd treat it like real work: agree the scope first, share progress, and deliver something you can actually run. I've built a whole Android app from zero to launch in four weeks at Kezhi, so I'm used to working fast with a clear goal.

question: What is something you changed your opinion about in the last year?
expected: 例如控制改动范围（主管反馈）或 AI 工具使用
answer: I used to think a better model would mostly decide how good an AI product is. Now I think the experience around it matters just as much: how fast you see something, what happens when it's wrong, and when it asks you first. At KKday, showing day one of the trip right away changed how the planner felt more than any model change.

question: How do you balance family and a demanding job?
expected: 陪孩子与家人是真实动机；冲刺时会投入，平时规律

I keep fixed working hours, and I do focused work in the morning. If a launch needs extra time, I'm there. If a family commitment affects my availability, I tell the team early and make sure my work is covered. I also prefer remote work, but I'm happy to work from Beijing and go back to Shanghai every month or two. So I take both my family and my commitments to the team seriously.

question: Tell me about the hardest bug you've ever fixed, in simple terms.
expected: 具体例子、简单英语，不展开技术细节到技术面
answer: The hardest bug was at KKday, on the product page. When a traveller tapped a date or ticket type, the price and stock took about a second to update. I found the app was recalculating every combination on the main thread and parsing the same JSON again and again. So I prepared the price and stock lookups in advance, moved the heavy work to a background thread, and sent results back through StateFlow. It dropped to about 300 milliseconds, and switching options felt smooth.
